title: HPV and You
summary: Josh and Chuck explain HPV (human papillomavirus), a very common sexually transmitted infection and the first virus shown to cause cancer. They cover cutaneous versus mucosal types, high-risk versus low-risk strains, genital warts and their treatment, HPV-related cancers (especially cervical and oropharyngeal), cervical cancer screening guidelines (PAP and HPV tests), the history of the HPV vaccines (Gardasil, Cervarix, Gardasil 9), Rick Perry's 2007 Texas mandate and vaccine hesitancy, and vaccination statistics. The episode ends with listener mail about the song "Wind of Change" by the Scorpions and a movie recommendation.

segments.title: Opening banter and HPV introduction
segments.summary: The hosts joke about an intro and introduce HPV as a very common sexually transmitted infection and the first virus found to cause cancer, noting an effective vaccine exists.

segments.title: History of HPV, warts, and cervical cancer
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the history of warts being linked to an infection, the 1917 German experiment on genital warts, 19th-century observations of cervical cancer among nuns and married women, and Harald zur Hausen's 1983 discovery of HPV16 in cervical cancer biopsies. They note HPV is species-specific and that HPV16 may have come from Neanderthals and Denisovans.

segments.title: Nobel Prize and viruses causing cancer
segments.summary: Zur Hausen's 1983 work is tied to his 2008 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. HPV is described as the first virus shown to cause cancer, with a note on viruses' possible role in other diseases.

segments.title: Cutaneous vs mucosal HPV and high-risk vs low-risk types
segments.summary: HPV types are divided into cutaneous types, which cause skin warts, and mucosal types, which infect moist areas and can spread sexually. Mucosal types are further classed as high-risk, which can lead to cancer, or low-risk, which almost never does. HPV spreads without exchange of body fluids, so condoms only partly help.

segments.title: HPV prevalence and infection rates
segments.summary: The hosts cite about 14 million new US infections a year and at least 80 million Americans currently infected, and speculate on a surge tied to changes in sexual mores and behavior.

segments.title: Genital warts, respiratory papillomatosis, and treatment
segments.summary: Low-risk mucosal HPV types 6 and 11 cause genital warts, which can be removed with medication, liquid nitrogen, or lasers. Respiratory papillomatosis, warts in the airway mainly in young children, can narrow the airway and is treated surgically. The mechanism of HPV replication and localized lesions is also described.

segments.title: HPV-related cancers
segments.summary: The hosts cite CDC data from 2021 showing about 37,000 HPV-associated cancers per year, 22,000 in women and 16,000 in men, including cervical, anal, penile, vaginal, vulvar, and oropharyngeal cancers. HPV16 and HPV18 are the most common cancer-causing types, with HPV16 responsible for about 90 percent of HPV-related oropharyngeal cancers and half of cervical cancers.

segments.title: Cervical cancer screening and declining rates
segments.summary: Cervical cancer deaths in the US have fallen by more than half from the mid-1970s to mid-2000s due to screening. Guidelines differ: the USPSTF recommends PAP tests from age 21 and not routine HPV testing under 30, while the American Cancer Society recommends starting at 25 with HPV testing. Abnormal results lead to colposcopy, biopsy, or monitoring. Screening is far less robust in some developing countries.

segments.title: Oropharyngeal cancer and oral sex
segments.summary: Tobacco-related oropharyngeal cancer is falling, but HPV-related cases are rising, with oral sex now the biggest risk factor and more oral partners raising risk. The hosts mention Michael Douglas's comments and researchers' interest in the problem.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: A short break before the vaccine discussion, with a note on other HPV-linked cancers that are rarer.

segments.title: HPV vaccine history and dosing
segments.summary: Jian Zhou and Ian Frazer at the University of Queensland developed the approach of using HPV16 proteins in a vaccine. The first vaccine, Gardasil, came out in 2006 and was approved for girls and women 9 to 26. It covered HPV 6, 11, 16, and 18. The FDA licensed it for boys and men in 2009. GlaxoSmithKline released Cervarix, Merck released Gardasil 9 in 2014, and the vaccine does not cure existing infections. Dosing is two shots for younger kids and three for those over 15.

segments.title: Vaccine controversy and Rick Perry's Texas mandate
segments.summary: The HPV vaccine launched amid autism-vaccine controversy. Texas governor Rick Perry mandated the vaccine for sixth-grade girls in 2007, which drew criticism over his ties to Merck. Studies found no increase in sexual behavior among vaccinated girls. Boys' vaccination was debated after a 2011 New York Times story, and later evidence showed straight men are at risk for oropharyngeal cancer.

segments.title: Vaccination benefits, coverage, and state requirements
segments.summary: Johns Hopkins modeling projected about 1,000 fewer oropharyngeal cancers by 2045 from male vaccination, limited by low male uptake. A 2021 study found 87 percent fewer cervical cancer cases among women vaccinated at 12 to 13. In 2022, 57 percent of 15-to-17-year-olds had at least one dose. Delaware, Rhode Island, Hawaii, Virginia, and DC require the vaccine for students.

segments.title: Closing HPV remarks
segments.summary: Josh wraps up the HPV episode and advises listeners to read from trusted sources.

segments.title: Listener mail on Scorpions' Wind of Change
segments.summary: Jimmy from Spokane writes about the Scorpions' song Wind of Change and the conspiracy theory that the CIA helped write it as Cold War propaganda. The hosts discuss the band, the Moscow Music Peace Festival, and a recommended podcast. Jimmy also recommends the 1978 Scorpions video Sails of Charon.

segments.title: Movie recommendation and closing
segments.summary: Josh recommends the 1979 horror film Tourist Trap, and Chuck mentions the Scorpions video. The hosts close with a listener mail call-out.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts ask listeners to send listener mail and close the show.
